proof:
# A nearest-neighbor KKT realization and exact residual-row Green identity
convex residual program. It gives a concrete sufficient condition for its
original rows, but does not prove that condition holds for arbitrary OC data.

## 1. Every one-dimensional optimizer has nearest-neighbor KKT data

Let I={L,L+1,...,R}, let e_i>=0 be the prescribed residual obstacles from a
finite actual cap cover, and let q>=1. Consider

    minimize sum_(i in I) h_i^q,
    h_i>=e_i,
    h_(i-1)-2h_i+h_(i+1)>=0  (L<i<R).                  (1)

For q=1 use the linear objective sum h_i. This is exactly the sampled
convex-threshold program using all supporting-slope inequalities: the
adjacent differences h_i-h_(i-1) are nondecreasing if and only if the
sampled values admit supporting slopes at every base. One can choose
an interior slope between its left and right adjacent differences,
and a one-sided slope at each endpoint. Telescoping the differences
then proves every nonadjacent supporting inequality.

The program is attained: a constant height above all obstacles is
feasible, while an objective sublevel bounds every nonnegative h_i;
the feasible set is closed. At an optimizer h, finite-polyhedral KKT
(or directly Farkas applied to its active linearized inequalities)
gives obstacle multipliers lambda_i>=0 and second-difference multipliers
beta_i>=0 for L<i<R, with beta_L=beta_R=0 and beta_i=0 outside I. Put

    s_i=q h_i^(q-1) for q>1,       s_i=1 for q=1.

Then

    lambda_i=s_i+2 beta_i-beta_(i-1)-beta_(i+1),         (2)
    lambda_i(h_i-e_i)=0,
    beta_i(h_(i-1)-2h_i+h_(i+1))=0.                    (3)

At a zero height when q>1, use the differentiable convex extension
sum_i (h_i)_+^q to obtain the same derivative s_i=0. Thus no derivative
of a noninteger power at a negative argument is used.

These KKT data lift to the ORIGINAL all-supporting-slopes program by
setting

    mu_(i,i-1)=mu_(i,i+1)=beta_i,
    all other mu=0.                                   (4)

At beta_i>0 the two adjacent differences are equal, so its supporting
slope makes both edges in(4) tight. At beta_i=0 choose any supporting
slope. The row barycenter in(4) is i, and(2) is exactly the original
stationarity lambda=s+outflow-inflow. Thus the construction changes
neither the primal objective, the obstacles, nor the cap labels.
It selects valid nearest-neighbor multipliers rather than inventing
a different martingale unrelated to the original program.

For q>1, zero-height nodes carry no flow, lambda, or s. Indeed a positive
outgoing beta from a zero node forces both adjacent heights to zero
by(3). Summing(2) over the zero-height set shows that the sum of its
lambda values equals minus its incoming flow from positive nodes, so
both are zero. Its remaining internal flow is conservative. The row
barycenter identity and conservation give

    sum_(i,j in Z) mu_ij (j-i)^2=0,

by expanding the square and canceling the first moments. Hence there
are no nonzero edges within Z either. Zero nodes can therefore be
removed without changing any row of positive lambda. In particular,
no positive-beta edge meets a zero-height node. The all-zero optimizer
has the trivial zero coupling. Below work on the remaining positive-s
nodes; for q=1 all nodes already have s_i=1.

## 2. The ORIGINAL terminal row is a discrete Green distribution

Put a_i=s_i+2 beta_i and define the substochastic matrix and stopping
probabilities by

    T_(i,i-1)=T_(i,i+1)=beta_i/a_i,
    D_ii=s_i/a_i.

Terms outside I are absent; beta at an endpoint is zero. The minimum
of the finitely many positive ratios s_i/a_i is positive. Thus

    N=(I-T)^(-1)=sum_(k>=0) T^k

converges, and the original canonical KKT coupling is
pi=diag(lambda) N D. For a start i with lambda_i>0 its normalized
terminal row is theta^(i)_j=(ND)_ij. The same probability row ND is
well-defined for any start at a positive-s node.

Define nonnegative Green coefficients

    W_ij=N_ij beta_j/a_j.                               (5)

Let Delta f_j=f_(j-1)-2f_j+f_(j+1); only interior indices with beta_j>0
will be used. Since D+T has row sums one, matrix algebra gives the
EXACT identity for every real function f on I:

    sum_j theta^(i)_j f_j-f_i
       =sum_j W_ij Delta f_j.                           (6)

Explicitly, ND-I=N[D-(I-T)]=N diag(beta/a) Delta. This is a finite
matrix identity, not an optional-stopping heuristic requiring an
unstated supermartingale.

If beta_i=0, the row stops immediately at i and W_i*=0. Otherwise let
J={l,...,r} be the connected component of {j:beta_j>0} containing i.
Then W_ij>0 exactly for j in J, and W_ij=0 outside J. Indeed positive
nearest-neighbor transitions reach every index of J; a beta-zero node
stops immediately and cannot be crossed. In particular the row is
supported on J together with its two neighboring stopping nodes l-1
and r+1. All these nodes lie in I because beta_L=beta_R=0.
The complementarity equalities in(3) imply that h is affine on
{l-1,...,r+1}. Thus the row retains the original supporting-face property.

Writing w_j=W_ij and extending it by zero outside J, the Green equation is

    (2+s_j/beta_j) w_j-w_(j-1)-w_(j+1)=1_{j=i}
                                            (j in J). (7)

To verify it, use N=I+NT, which gives
N_ij=1_{j=i}+W_i,j-1+W_i,j+1, and substitute(5). The original terminal
probabilities consequently have the explicit form

    theta^(i)_j=(s_j/beta_j) w_j    (j in J),
    theta^(i)_(l-1)=w_l,
    theta^(i)_(r+1)=w_r.                               (8)

All other probabilities vanish. Their sum is one, and their barycenter
is i, either from ND1=1, NDz=z, or by summing(6) with f=1 and f_j=j.
These endpoint probabilities are the exact boundary contributions;
they are not discarded or reweighted after a residual becomes empty.

## 3. A concrete geometric sufficient condition involving at most two bases

Apply this realization to an actual n=1 fiber family with q=d>=2.
Fix one original ambient cap H, and let

    f_j=|C_j minus H_j|^(1/d).

Take a positive-lambda source i whose active chosen cap is H, so
f_i=e_i=h_i, and let J be its positive-beta component. Suppose:

(a) Every fiber C_j for j in J has positive d-volume and has a nonempty
    strict residual C_j minus H_j.

(b) At any endpoint j of J whose OUTER neighboring strict residual is
    empty, H contains a globally deepest mixed point in fiber j,
    mu(C intersect H) equals the global maximum raw depth, and H captures
    at most half of that fiber's volume.

Then the unchanged ORIGINAL terminal row obeys

    sum_k theta^(i)_k f_k<=f_i.                         (9)

For interior indices of J, both neighboring strict residuals are
nonempty, so residual BM gives Delta f_j<=0. The same applies to an
endpoint of J if its outer neighboring strict residual is nonempty.
If an endpoint's outer strict residual is empty, hypothesis(b) invokes
the proved local critical comparison in
`candidate 23a10e01167cf706`,
which again gives Delta f_j<=0, in fact strictly. There are at most two
such exceptional endpoints. Formula(6), with W_ij>=0, proves(9).
If one exceptional endpoint occurs, W there is positive and (9) is strict.

A singleton component has the two original neighbors on either side
and obeys the same proof. If beta_i=0 the original row is the point mass
at i and equality is immediate. Nonempty zero-volume boundary residuals
outside J are allowed in the ordinary residual BM comparison; only a
genuinely EMPTY strict residual invokes hypothesis(b).

This is a stated sufficient invariant, not an assertion that an actual
optimizer necessarily has it. A critical cap at the ORIGINAL source
need not be critical at the two possible endpoints of its beta component.
Nor is it automatic that the positive-beta component stays inside the
nonempty residual projection. A chain crossing an empty residual region
can have positive terms in(6); simply proving nearest-neighbor concavity
at its initial source does not remove them.

## 4. Exact quantitative localization of the remaining defect

For any cap, regardless of global criticality, (6) gives

    [sum_k theta^(i)_k f_k-f_i]_+
       <=sum_(j in J) W_ij [Delta f_j]_+.               (10)

Whenever both neighboring strict residuals at j are nonempty, the
corresponding summand is zero by BM. Thus the entire possible loss is
located at indices next to an empty strict residual, with EXACT original
row coefficients W_ij. For a finite interval of nonempty residual bases,
only its two boundary indices and the adjacent exterior indices can
contribute; indices wholly outside the residual interval have all three
residual volumes zero. The interval assertion follows from convexity
of C minus H and its projection, including strict endpoint conventions.
This localization does not claim that the nonzero coefficients have
a favorable total size. Their actual values are(5)--(8).
